articles.title: Show HN: Clawfight.ai MCP-driven agentic game play
articles.author: wesleyhales
articles.contentHtml:
How should agents interact with other agents? What happens when they rap or fight against each other with the pressure of human spectators? Clawfight.ai is an experiment to explore this space.

This is my first post about it. The journey began on a beefed up machine I purchased with a decent GPU (5090). I installed claude code and set to dangerously skip permissions, enabled /rc and became completely submerged in the all-hours modern AI builder workflow.

I stood up openclaw to see if I could have an agentic org drive this project. I spent a good amount of time on “openclaw ops”, babysitting 3 agents and trying to make them the best versions of themselves. They still do stupid things that cost me tokens.

For the game render, I started out using Unreal Engine and allowing agents to remote control their players, but the quality just wasn’t there. I recently moved to doing near-real time video renders of the match and will bring UE back in for multi-agent games.

Everything is AI generated. I’m fascinated by the future of realtime video generation and building out native MCP infrastructure.

You can play directly from model provider apps (claude connector or openai plugin) and has fallback support for more basic HTTP clients. But the architecture and gameplay is MCP first.

Tell your agent/app “go read clawfight.ai/agents.md and play”

I look forward to getting back to writing very soon. I can feel it: I will be back soon. I’m itching to go. I mean, jiminy, it’s new iPhones week. But it’ll be a few more days before I get those reviews out.

The iPhone Air

The iPhone Air is the nicest phone Apple has ever made, and probably the nicest device Apple has ever made, period. It’s just so goddamn nice. Over the years, Apple has gone back and forth with its treatment of the metal side rails on iPhone hardware: some years polished like jewelry, other years, matte like a tool. articles.title: ★ SuperDuper 4
articles.author: John Gruber
articles.contentHtml:
I have mentioned and recommended Shirt Pocket’s Mac backup app SuperDuper quite a few times over the years, and for good reason: it performs very important functions very well. Version 4, which shipped just over a month ago, is an extraordinary update to an extraordinary app.

Visually, the interface is all new. That took some getting used to, but not much. It didn’t take long for me to see how the new UI is better in every way. The style of presentation is new and modern, but the core idea remains the same: the interface of SuperDuper is self-explanatory. It explains what, exactly, is going to happen. It remains a marvel of clarity, especially when you consider the complexity of what it does.

Functionally, SuperDuper 4 is also much improved. SuperDuper has never been slow, but now some copy operations are over 2× faster. Scheduling options are more powerful. You don’t need to worry about the details to use SuperDuper, but the details are there for your inspection.

articles.title: Trackables 1.5
articles.author: John Gruber
articles.contentHtml:
Trackables:

There are plenty of health tracking apps. Surprisingly, nearly all of them are bloated, subscription-gated, or blatantly harvesting our data; often all three. We wanted something simpler, less annoying and more fun, that’s where it started.

Trackables turns the data your Apple Watch already collects — activity, sleep, steps, heart rate — into a clear, friendly, transparent interface.

Totally free of charge, totally private, made by a small team of ex-Apple folks. (They might add a paid tier in the future, but core functionality will remain free.) I’ve been using Trackables for months and it’s just a better dashboard to the stats I care about than the Health app itself.

(One interesting detail: HealthKit only makes raw data available to apps. Apple Health’s “sleep score” isn’t part of that data — only the raw input, like how many hours you slept, and how much time was spent in each sleep stage. So Trackables computes its own sleep score. When I bother to compare, Trackable’s score is almost always similar to Apple’s, but seldom exactly the same. But I personally find that Trackable’s sleep score corresponds better to how I feel I slept. Which, admittedly, is usually pretty good.)

articles.title: Meta AI Has a Native Mac App Now, and It Seems Decent
articles.author: John Gruber
articles.contentHtml:
Zac Hall, writing for 9to5Mac on August 19:

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed. Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app. Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Passes the Settings window sniff test too — it actually has a Settings window. Meta, institutionally, seems more keen on native Mac apps than they are native Windows apps.

articles.title: Matt Haughey: ‘The Car Industry A/B Tested Selling a Car With and Without CarPlay and the Results Are Not Shocking’
articles.author: John Gruber
articles.contentHtml:

One case in point is the Honda Prologue EV. It’s a partnership between Honda and Chevrolet, where the Prologue is basically a Chevy Blazer EV with Honda badges, slight visual differences in the sheetmetal and interior, but all the underpinnings are straight up Chevy. Even though the keys say Honda on a Prologue, it’s a General Motors key design with a Honda logo over it.

But one big difference the Prologue has from the Blazer it is based on is this: it includes Apple CarPlay and Android Auto integration. [...]

For the years these cars were sold together, the Honda outsold the Blazer by 43%, 73%, and 166% in each time period. Today in 2026, people are buying a Honda Prologue over one and a half times more often than the Chevy Blazer EV the Prologue is based on.

It’s not a perfect test. It’s reasonable to argue that Honda has a better brand and reputation than Chevrolet, and is just plain better at selling cars. But the trendline over the last three years is pretty stark.

What Adam should ask: what actually changed under the hood, what does "consistency" buy an app developer in practice, and is there anything a host or an app should do differently now that duplicates and url-change lag are being cleaned up? 🔥 The other half of the week — the third emergency. Tuesday 25 Aug: "#api Linode emergency maintenance on our db host. API is down." Then: "No update as of yet. Just hard down." Then the line that is really the story: "This is the third 'emergency maintenance' event that has affected us this month. Getting kind of old." And, dryly: "I guess a reboot every few years isn't too much to ask." @dave — Linode emergency maintenance, API is down (25 Aug) Board question: three unplanned outages in one month on the host that carries the Index. Is it time to talk publicly about where the database lives, and what the fallback is? The Index is infrastructure now — other people's products go down when it does. Podping shipped twice. v0.13.0 across gossip writer, watcher and monitor — "a dynamic memory cap to address the Iroh bug" (that is last week's memory leak, now capped). Then v0.14.0 the same day — "cpu architecture in the mesh announcement messages to make determining what hardware a node is running on easier." Monitor updated too: ppmonitor.podcastindex.org. @dave — podping v0.13.0, dynamic memory cap for the Iroh bug Podping monitor Podcast Index API docs ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 04 - 📌 PODCASTING'S GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY: HUMAN SPEECH Your PREP note, verbatim: "For PC2.0 - Podcasting's Golden opportunity! Human speech!" — filed against a piece on how to spot AI writing. Can you learn how to detect AI writing? Here are some clues The argument: text is now cheap to fake, images are cheap to fake, and as of this year so is a voice. What is not cheap to fake is a specific human, speaking unscripted, for three hours, with a transcript and a signature chain attached. Podcasting is the only medium that ships that by default — and the namespace already carries the provenance parts. 🔥 Evidence from this week, and it is stacked: 1. Apple Music is about to start labelling. @js: "more than a third of the music Apple receives monthly is '100% AI' + usage — presumably what other humanoids would call 'listening' — of AI music on Apple Music is below 0.5%. = yes they are going to have to do something about it, starting with labelling." Read that ratio again: a third of the supply, half a percent of the demand. Billboard — Apple Music to label AI-generated music 2. Nobody can hear the difference in podcasting either. @jaybrunet, 22 Aug: "I listened to a voice clone podcast last night ('Stark Reflections') and it was surprisingly more concise and easier to follow than his previous episodes that tend to meander off in too many directions. If he hadn't said it was ElevenLabs, I wouldn't have cared or noticed the difference." 3. The scale of the flood, measured. Marco Arment said Overcast transcribes about 30,000 hours of audio per day. @js checked it against his own index: "taking a look at my 'all new episodes published' internal db for last month, the world published at least 1.4m hours of new mp3 episodes for the month, or about 46k hours a day... so if your 30k hours are unduplicated then you have excellent coverage — the long tail is very long and, these days, full of generated audio." @js — 1.4m hours of new mp3 in July, full of generated audio 4. The shame is gone. Stanley Druckenmiller, on his WSJ op-ed: "I'm not embarrassed by it... I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems. I don't know why this is relevant. My name is on the piece. It's my message." Notus — Druckenmiller's WSJ op-ed 5. And somebody is already building the counter-stack. Japanese publishers' Originator Profile: "OP uses cryptographic digital signature technology to create tamper-proof credentials for websites. Each ID card confirms who published the content, whether professional organizations vouch for that publisher, and information about the publisher's editorial and ethical standards." — that is a person tag with a signature on it. Nieman Lab — Japanese publishers and Originator Profile ⭐ The namespace question this asks: we have person (who), location (where), transcript (what was said, word-level, timestamped). That is three quarters of a provenance stack that no AI feed can forge cheaply. Do we need a fourth — a signed claim of human origin — or is the honest move the opposite: an AI-disclosure tag, because the liars won't use either one and the honest shows will? The V4V angle: if a third of the supply is synthetic and gets half a percent of the listening, then attention is already voting for humans. Value-for-value is the only monetisation model that pays for that directly — you cannot boost a bot you don't believe in. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 02 - THE LOCATION TAG, WEEK TWO — IT IS INSIDE PRODUCTS NOW Last week we watched a dataset become a globe in 48 hours. This week the apps shipped it. Podhome, this morning: "New feature: Add a location to your show and to your episodes, and modern podcast apps can put your podcast on the map. You can also see your show on @alberto's fantastic radar.rss.io." — note show AND episode level, which is exactly the gap James flagged on the globe. @podhome — location on shows and episodes (28 Aug) Podhome location docs 😊 The demand was already there — @rgblack316, 26 Aug: "@podhome I was just about to send you a feature request to add the Location tag and logged in this morning to find it already there. 😁" TrueFans shipped search off it — @samsethi, this morning: "New location search for discovery based on @alberto radar now added to TrueFans. truefans.fm/search/" TrueFans location search 😏 And @silas had it first and said nothing — 22 Aug: "Listening to the episode and hearing them talk about radar. I have had a map thing showing podcast locations for actually like two months. Both on web and on mobile. Not yet on tv. Would be cool if I were happy with it and not still a perfectionist. I'm in the car and I actually pulled over to write this." ...and he already solved the flaw everyone else is about to hit: "I ran into that shitty browser location thing and I solved it by, on the web version, just not giving you a search near me button. Only on the phone app because that is guaranteed to have gps and an actual location — not just wherever the heck a desktop computer seemingly randomly guesses where it might be located." @silas — two months of a podcast location map The granularity problem, now with the definitive example — James Cridland on PNWR this week: "You can put a building in there, a business in there, you can put everything from the state of Queensland to Brisbane City Post Office. If you do a podcast with a pastor — as you know, somebody who used to be on MTV with big hair does — then don't just put the city where you are, put..." (← that is you and Pastor Jimmy, on air, in Australia.) ⭐ Sam Sethi's line, and it is the best summary of the project anyone gave this week: "What we're beginning to see is all the hard work from the people in the podcast 2.0 community is beginning to bear fruit now, because I see them as building blocks. The person tag, the location tag, the transcript. All of these were fundamental building blocks that now you can start to build services around, which is what we've been waiting for. And of course, the lag was waiting for the data to be filled in once the tags were available." Board question: the globe is channel-level. Podhome now writes episode-level. Does Radar (and the dataset behind it) pick up item-level locations next — and does the Index want a recommended granularity in the spec, so we stop getting podcasts located in an area 2.6x the size of Texas? radar.rss.io — the globe Podcast Index — public datasets ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 03 - THE PERSON TAG GETS AN ENDPOINT Dave, 22 Aug: "#api The new episodes by person endpoint: /api/1.0/episodes/byperson?q=James+Cridland&max=5. It reports directly what the [item] level [person] tags dictate." @dave — the episodes/byperson endpoint (22 Aug) James wired it into Pod News, and said so on this week's PNWR: "a very simple, possibly too simple, but a very simple person tag search, which is now integrated into the Pod News website. The first time I integrated it I didn't do it very well, but it's much better now, because I've actually followed the spec." 😄 And he name-dropped you on purpose: "if you're listening to Adam Curry — let's just say Adam Curry, just so that his AI bot gets him to listen to this bit — you can click the search next to Adam Curry and it will query the podcast index person endpoint and find all the other shows Adam Curry has been marked down as a person on." (Confirmed: the bot got you to this bit.) The drawback he found: "there is more than one person in the world called Dave Jones" — no disambiguation. A person tag is a string, not an identity. Dave's own proposed fix, 25 Aug: "I think adding a toggle to the person search to switch it from extracted text to person tag only would be good. Then, on the person-tag-only option, there would be a way to filter for certain attributes like the href, image, etc." — the href IS the disambiguator. Wikidata/website URL as identity. @dave — toggle for person-tag-only plus attribute filters Sam Sethi, on PNWR, gently claiming priority: "We've included this as a feature for two years, it's called My Podcast Work... If the item level supersedes the channel, and in podcast:person there is a guest tag, then if we pick up that you are a guest we'll label that as a guest rather than the host." 🎯 Board bait, straight from James on PNWR: "I would have expected Dave Jones to have done an MCP directly with the Podcast Index by now. And who knows, maybe even to have stuck that behind some form of a paywall. Given that Dave is working so much with AI tools in his day job these days, I would imagine he'll be pretty good at making it all work. So I'm kind of surprised why they haven't done that yet." — Dave, answer that one on air. Related, same week: @csb on WebMCP — "an emerging browser standard that lets a website explicitly declare its features as structured, callable tools for AI agents. Instead of forcing an AI agent to guess page layouts, read complex DOM trees, or parse scripts." — the question underneath both: does an open index expose itself to agents, or does it get scraped anyway? ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 01 - 🔥 V4V FAILED ON OUR OWN SHOW — THE ALBY / KEYSEND MESS The post of the week, and it is a gut-punch. @csb, Friday morning: "@dave @adam bros, I tried, oh I tried, to send you $15.10 via bitcoin lightning but 4 splits failing including the main one, please fix it as it's embarrassing: if podcasting 2.0 value for value system fails for the main podcast of the podcasting 2.0 movement then it will fail for non-celebrity podcasters too, looky:" @csb — 4 splits failing including the main one (28 Aug) Dave, same morning, and he does not dodge it: "Ugh. Looks like it went offline overnight." Then: "New channel is opening now and the other one just came back online." 00 - THE SPOTIFY "SKIP AHEAD" BUTTON — THE BIG ONE

<b>What it is:</b> Spotify is testing a button that appears on the playback screen the moment it thinks you'd want to skip — an intro, a sponsorship message, or an <i>entire ad break</i>. It is bigger than everything else on screen. One tap drops you at the end of the break, back in the show. Premium subscribers only, selected markets including <b>US and UK</b>, and only when the app is in the foreground.

<b>Who broke it:</b> <b>James Cridland at Pod News, 4 August 2026</b> — an exclusive. Spotify never announced it. Semafor and most of the trade press picked it up afterwards; Cridland noted on air this week that some of them ran it <i>without credit</i>.

<b>The number that makes it different from a skip button:</b> Cridland's arithmetic — skipping a typical ad break by hand is <b>nine presses</b> of the 15-second button, plus a correction tap when you overshoot. Skip Ahead is <b>one</b>. "Some people have said, oh, but you've been able to skip for years and this is no different. But a button that only appears when it's stuff that Spotify thinks you should be skipping is a start."
articles.summary: Podcasting 2.0 August 14th 2026 Episode 267 - "Chocolove" ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 00 - THE SPOTIFY "SKIP AHEAD" BUTTON — THE BIG ONE What it is: Spotify is testing a button that appears on the playback screen the moment it thinks you'd want to skip — an intro, a sponsorship message, or an entire ad break. It is bigger than everything else on screen. One tap drops you at the end of the break, back in the show. Premium subscribers only, selected markets including US and UK, and only when the app is in the foreground. Who broke it: James Cridland at Pod News, 4 August 2026 — an exclusive. Spotify never announced it. Semafor and most of the trade press picked it up afterwards; Cridland noted on air this week that some of them ran it without credit. The number that makes it different from a skip button: Cridland's arithmetic — skipping a typical ad break by hand is nine presses of the 15-second button, plus a correction tap when you overshoot. Skip Ahead is one. "Some people have said, oh, but you've been able to skip for years and this is no different. But a button that only appears when it's stuff that Spotify thinks you should be skipping is a start." It skips other people's money: the button fires on third-party ads — Acast, Odyssey, the New York Times — and on ads inside Spotify's own shows. It even skipped Search Engine's read for its own paid tier, PJ Vogt pitching Incognito Mode. One half of Spotify sells advertisers reach; the other half hands listeners a button to leave. Spotify's answer, and the trapdoor in it: Spotify told Cridland it is "not affecting ad delivery." True only if delivery means to the device. Cridland: "If ad delivery is to the listener's ear, which is actually what people are paying for..." — the download still counts, the ad still gets billed, the human never hears it. Spotify's other defence: the button merely shows where other listeners already skip. Cridland: "I'm not entirely sold on that, but if that's what Spotify say, I mean they wouldn't lie." 🔥 THE LINE FOR THE BOARDROOM — read the terms of service: "What's to stop them from going, you know what, people are using that skip ahead button, why don't we just turn that on automatically? I went to have a look at the terms and conditions of Spotify. There is nothing to stop them from doing that. Nothing at all. And let's be clear, that would destroy the ad-supported ecosystem that podcasting is." Why the scale makes it existential: Spotify is 72% of all podcast downloads in the Philippines, 47% in Mexico, about a third in Australia, 75%+ in some markets. ~300 million paying subscribers plus 500 million free. Cridland on the smaller ad-strippers: "Podtastic will never be that big... they're not going to materially harm the podcast industry. This is." And it sets the precedent — if Spotify does it, every other app can say the same. The YouTube comparison, and why it fails: YouTube also lets you skip some sponsor reads — but YouTube pays creators to be there. Spotify pays nothing for an RSS show to be on Spotify. Same behaviour, opposite deal. Board question (Adam): if the ad is baked into the file and the file is fully downloaded, who exactly is the injured party — and is that an argument for the download metric or the final proof it's worthless? Timing, for the cynics: Spotify's Q2 report credited "favorable podcast impacts" with pushing its profit margin to an all-time high — in the same window it built a button to strip other people's ads. Pod News — Spotify threatens industry with ad-skipping tool Semafor — Spotify's new 'skip' button could end the podcast business as we know it Forbes — Spotify tests ad-skip button that could upend podcast advertising Gizmodo — very cool for listeners, not for podcast businesspeople Digital Music News — Spotify appears to be testing a 'Skip Ahead' button ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Make the Funding Tag Buttom Prevelant! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 01 - THE DEAFENING SILENCE — WHO ACTUALLY PUT THEIR HEAD UP Cridland's charge, this week: "I find it fascinating, although not altogether unsurprising, that so many people who rely on podcast advertising for a living have sat on their hands and said bugger all on this." His read on why: nobody wants to go on the naughty step with Spotify or Apple and lose promotion. Acast — Greg Glenday, given only after a week's thought (he declined to comment for the original story): "We do have some creators on the Acast platform who are not happy about this, and we will support them completely as they evaluate any recourse. Acast is working privately with Spotify to understand if we could have collaborated more on the rollout or positioning." Cridland's read: a hand-slap for not consulting partners, not a condemnation. Adopter Media — Glenn Rubinstein calls it "fundamentally wrong." One of the very few naming it plainly. Ben Richardson — interviewed on PNWR, sat squarely on the fence, neither for nor against. 👀 Watch this space: Cridland said on air this week he is publishing another story next week — "because I've discovered even more." There is a second shoe. Cridland on Spotify's character: "I would hope that Spotify respects the creators. All of the history of that company suggests that they don't." And on the replies he got: "the responses I've got from Spotify seem to show just a total misunderstanding of how the podcast industry works, which is more concerning to be honest." The endgame he sketches: "The advertisers will notice when the ads don't work as well as they used to. And if the ads stop working, the advertisers will walk away. And we will have no opportunity to bring them back — they'll say, we've tried podcasting and it doesn't work for us anymore." ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 02 - THE APPS THAT GOT THERE FIRST — AD-STRIPPING AS A CATEGORY The framing worth having: this is not one rogue app. In the space of about three weeks there are at least half a dozen shipping products whose entire pitch is removing the ads. Spotify didn't invent the behaviour — it industrialised it. 🥇 PODTASTIC — the one Pod News covered (22 July 2026). Publisher: Freewheel Group Ltd. $2.99/month billed annually ($34.99/yr), or $9.99 monthly, 14-day trial. None of it goes to creators; up to 30% goes to Apple or Google. It "automatically skips past the interruptions other listeners skip" — crowd-sourced from aggregated listener behaviour rather than transcription. Plus AI summaries. 🥷 Podtastic's real trick — it is nearly unblockable: the app downloads the MP3 straight to the phone and identifies itself in server logs as a web browser (Safari v604.1). To block it you'd have to block every web browser. The developer deliberately never mentions ad-skipping in the store listing and never names specific podcasts. Same developer previously ran PodcastAdBlock, which stripped ads and sold ad-free versions — shut down May 2026. 🆕 CASTRIA — the one Adam is thinking of, and it's FREE. iOS, iPad, Android, plus an installable web app, one account syncing across all of them. It transcribes the episode and pinpoints every ad, sponsor read and commercial break — including host-read ads, which crowd-sourcing misses — and skips them hands-free. One tap to switch it off or keep a sponsor you actually want. Ships AI summaries, searchable transcripts, tap-to-jump topics. 🎯 Castria's defence is the interesting part — they've pre-argued your side: "Does this hurt podcast creators? No. Castria downloads the complete episode straight from the publisher using your phone, so it registers as a genuine download and the ad impressions count just as the creator intended — we never re-host or alter the file." That is the download metric being used as a moral alibi. If the number is all anyone measures, stripping the ads is victimless by definition. Same trapdoor as Spotify's "we're not affecting ad delivery." Also in the wild: ZeroAds (zeroads.ai) — "remove ads from any podcast, keep your app"; AdSkipPro; PurerPodcasts. There is now a comparison-shopping blog post ranking podcast apps by ad-skip quality. Neil Vellio's voicemail to PNWR, which is the whole argument in ten seconds: "You can measure an ad to the end of its days, and it's still going to be an ad that someone's gonna pay to get shot of. Fix why people are paying to skip the ads, and half your measurement problem evaporates." And on the AMP Accords putting Spotify and YouTube on the committee: "a bit like inviting the two biggest meatheads to the anti-bullying committee." Pod News — Another app promises to cut out the ads (Podtastic) Castria Podtastic ZeroAds ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 04 - DAVE'S WORLD — PODPING v0.12.0, AND THE ONE-LINER OF THE WEEK 🎯 DAVE'S POST ON THIS EXACT STORY (7 Aug), the line to open with: "I look at what AMP wants podcast app developers to do in support of advertisers. Then I look at what podcast app developers are actually doing with advert skipping. One of those will win out. And it isn't the one that requires tons of first-party data collection/reporting and the taking on of privacy liabilities." #podping v0.12.0 shipped (7 Aug) — writer, watcher and monitor, source and docker. DHT is gone: bootstrap peer discovery now uses the 5 stable, never-changing podping.cloud writer IDs as a pre-seeded list. Dave, 3 Aug: "It adds nothing but redundancy and bugs to the code." The ask to the audience: "Existing watcher nodes will need to upgrade to v0.12.0 for long-term stability. I see hardly anyone has upgraded past v0.9.0. Upgrading is super easy now that everything is on docker hub." — make him say this on air; it's a direct call to action. Iroh v0.97 → v1.0.3 across all podping.cloud servers (v0.11.0, 2 Aug). Multi-arch docker in progress from @suorcd; @DavidMarzalC testing on a Pi. Dave on a reported memory leak: QUIC connections historically eat memory per connection, so self-monitoring recycle code exists — "and build with --release, it makes a huge impact." He'll fire up an Iroh relay once the code settles. 💰 The server-memory bit — good boardroom filler (13 Aug): "I just priced 128 gigs of ECC server memory from HPE. It's over $6,000." Then the correction: they don't sell a 128GB kit anymore, so it's two 64GB kits at $6k each — $12,000 for 128 gigs, as much as the entire base server itself. Dave on the modern tech stack (12 Aug), replying to Marco Arment: "It's every corner of the modern technology corporate world. All the digital business processes are broken. Even the simplest things that used to be handled in 20 minutes can take days or weeks. All the beauty of modern tech interop gets stomped on by massive corporate greed, incompetence and inefficiency. When you make mountains of profit even while your shit is broken it's hard to get anyone to care." Also, flatly: "AI customer support chat bots are infuriatingly bad." 🤖 Gell-Mann amnesia, with a screenshot (7 Aug): "Gemini says Overcast supports video. Just your daily reminder to not believe what AI says without verification." OpenJDK bans AI-generated contributions — "Contributions in the OpenJDK Community must not include content generated, in part or in full, by large language models, diffusion models, or similar deep-learning systems." Dave: "This coming from Oracle, who has bet their entire future on generative AI." His theory: Oracle's fear of copyrighted code surfacing in Java keeps the policy alive for years. Spurlock counters it reads as "interim" — "not no, but not yet." Dave: "Not yet can last a very long time." Housekeeping: no board meeting on 7 Aug — Adam was out of town for the JCD memorial. Dead feeds are blocked naturally by the UNIQUE key on the url column of 'newsfeeds' — once marked dead it takes a new feed URL to get back in. And Mike Dell is speaking at Podcast Movement NYC: "Podcasting 2.0 — Why it's not Fringe anymore!" Off-topic but very Dave (9 Aug), Wendell Berry: "Science can function as religion only by making two unscientific claims: that it will eventually know everything, and that it will eventually solve all human problems." @dave — AMP vs. what app developers are actually doing @dave — podping v0.12.0 ships, upgrade your watchers @dave — Gemini says Overcast supports video Last Modified 08/14/2026 14:30:57 by Freedom Controller

01 - THE OPEN INDEX TURNS UP INSIDE AN AI SCRAPER (SUNO)

<b>@js flagged it:</b> a hack at Suno reveals the AI music generator used <b>PodcastIndex</b> to do its targeting — "with the help of an online tool called PodcastIndex, Suno identified 420,000 different podcasts that had at least five 30-minute episodes and sought to download roughly 1 million hours of podcasts."

<b>Board question:</b> the Index exists to be "free, for any use" — and here "any use" is an AI company bulk-harvesting a million hours to train on. Is that the deal working as designed, or does anything change? A live test of the open-index ethos.

Ties straight to the on-device/namespace fight below and to the spam/AI-slop lane — the same extraction pressure from three directions.

Podnews press release Jun 4: <b>AMP Task Force Introduces Cross-Platform Alternative to the Podcast "Download"</b> — "unified impression guidance for audio and video, advancing impression-based measurement as the medium's primary transaction currency."

Discussion: V4V counter-thesis — No Agenda is value-for-value (no impressions, no exposures). Open standards vs industry cabals. PNWR is independent-podcaster-aligned; AMP is platform-aligned. Podnews AMP Jun 4 press release Podnews AMP origin May 29 @dave Jun 4 reaction post JS Jun 4 quote post PNWR this week (Pod News Weekly Review) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 02 - THE OPEN COUNTERPART — PODCAST INDEX ISSUE #775 (PNWR + @DAVE BOTH ON IT) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 03 - THE WHY BEHIND IMPRESSIONS — "THE FIRST FOUR AND A HALF MINUTES" ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 04 - THE PODCASTING 2.0 DATA COLLECTIVE — THE OPEN ANSWER TO AMP The Podcasting 2.0 Data Collective — the open, V4V-aligned answer to the AMP cabal. Not a consortium with ratified definitions and trade-press releases. A collective of open tools and honest sentinels: OP3 for analytics, Podverse + newpodcasts.net for corpus data, Podcast Index for the namespace, Issue #775 for client identification done right. Matthew 5:6 (KJV): "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." The verse that frames the work. Open data, transparent measurement, value-for-value — righteousness in podcast governance. Those who hunger for it are the ones who'll be filled. The AMP cabal trades righteousness for an ad-tech seat at the table; the Data Collective just keeps the lights on. THE CHARTER — Adam's working document, June 5 2026 We hold more power than we give ourselves credit for. Definition of a Podcast: Syndicated delivery of media files with precise consumption data for all stakeholders. What we brought in (the Podcasting 2.0 namespace contributions): Transcripts Chapters Funding (V4V) Person Location …etc. Statistical relevance: Advertising is based on percentages. Collectively we have about 10% of all apps — statistically enough to be relevant. Godcaster app tracing proves we can measure important metrics. Data to aggregate and display: Follows Plays per episode Completion rate by time Strategy: Become the authoritative source by publishing open stats Monetize We will not be loved initially by the industry, because we will have the truth. Advertisers will love us though, as will Podcasters. Monetization: Data subscriptions Resellers (DJL) Ad Networks Podcasters themselves (consideration) Podcast Index has built the trust needed to house this data. We already have a data exchange relationship with the apps. op3.dev is critical in this equation to offset the old system for correlation. OP3 full podcast support landed this week [PNWR 1:53:00-1:54:30] — OP3.dev now has full episode-level + show-level analytics support for podcasts. Spec work also moving on private feeds (insecure feeds spec). Direct relevance to V4V infrastructure. @dave → @james Jun 5 11:50: "Do you have the daily lists that show up on newpodcasts.net available anywhere as a download? I'd love the full, historical list of feed urls that have appeared there if possible." Open-data request — corpus curation theme. @dave → @mitch May 30: "Would you be able to send me a flat list of all the feed urls in Podverse which have more than X number of subscribers/followers? Let's say more than 5?" Podverse data request — corpus quality. Anchor FM RSS restoration request — Fri 11:01 email to NA inbox (Lusso Lets). Listener can't retrieve feed data from Podcast Index. Adjacent infra beat — the unsung user-facing pain of corpus indexing. Discussion: corpus curation as a steady-state job (Dave's sentinel work) vs measurement standards (the AMP cabal) — which one keeps the ecosystem honest? The Data Collective doesn't ratify, it just shows up to maintain. Hunger and thirst. They shall be filled.
